t: The Underground Railroad was neither literally underground nor a railroad: it had no headquarters or governing body, and consisted of meeting points, secret routes, transport and safe houses kept by sympathisers and passed on by word of mouth.

Free and enslaved African Americans were the main actors in the network, and most escapes from slavery had no help from an abolitionist; routes ran north to Canada, south to Mexico and Florida, to Native American lands and by sea to the Bahamas.

The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 drove thousands of African Americans to Canada, and historians debate how many escaped: estimates run from 100,000 by 1850 to 500,000 or more by the end of the Civil War.
dyk: The first known use of the term in print, on 10 August 1842, was a joke by the African American abolitionist Thomas Smallwood, who was quoting a Baltimore constable's exasperation that fugitives must be travelling by "steam balloon" or "underground rail-road".
ev: Enslaved Africans revolt at the Spanish colony of San Miguel de Gualdape, and historians suggest they escaped to Shakori Indigenous communities
The Spanish establish Fort Mose for free Blacks in the St. Augustine area of Spanish Florida
The original Fugitive Slave Act makes it easier to capture African Americans and return them to slavery, and spurs abolitionists to help the enslaved
Thomas Smallwood uses the term underground rail-road in print for the first time
The Compromise of 1850 brings a more stringent Fugitive Slave Law, and by December an estimated 3,000 African Americans have taken refuge in Canada
General Benjamin Butler keeps three men who fled to Fort Monroe, calling them contraband of war
President Abraham Lincoln issues the Emancipation Proclamation
The Thirteenth Amendment outlaws slavery except as punishment for a crime

f.where: the United States, from the slave states north to free states and Canada (above all Ontario), south to Florida and Mexico, and by sea to the Caribbean; routes also led into Indian territories and western territories
f.period: earlier escape routes from the 16th century; a network of safe houses organising from the 1780s among Northern abolitionist societies; growth to the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863; escapes to Union lines during the Civil War, 1861 to 1865
f.figures: Harriet Tubman, a conductor who had escaped slavery; William Still, who kept records and was sometimes called the Father of the Underground Railroad; Levi Coffin, said to have aided over 2,000 fugitives; Charles Turner Torrey; Thomas Smallwood; Thomas Downing; Mary Meachum; Silvia Hector Webber; Frederick Douglass, a critic of its publicity
f.outcome: estimates of those who escaped range from 100,000 by 1850 to 500,000 or more by the end of the Civil War; at least 30,000, and possibly more than 100,000, reached Canada; the network faded as the Emancipation Proclamation and the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery
